fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a very good question, and I want to be honest that I don't know. I think it's genuinely mysterious. But let me say a few things about it.

The thing that is striking to me is that the human value function clearly cares about things that are extremely high-level. Not just food, not just pain. It cares about things like, does this person think well of me? Am I being respected? Those are very complicated functions of the sensory input. And yet evolution somehow managed to attach a hardcoded reward to them, even though the genome is small and doesn't know anything about the particular neurons that will end up in any particular brain.

So here is one possibility. Maybe it's easier than it looks, because the brain is going to build that computation anyway. Any social animal has to learn to recognize faces, to read expressions, to model what the others around it want, because it needs that to survive. So evolution doesn't have to specify the computation. It only has to say: whatever this circuit outputs, when it says this person approves of you, make that feel good. And there is some evidence the brain is organized in this way. There are regions for processing faces, and they end up in roughly the same place in everyone. So maybe the genome can address them, like a slot that is fixed in advance and that learning then fills in.

Another possibility is that evolution bootstraps from something very simple. You start with something primitive, the infant's dependence on the parent, warmth, the mother's voice, some very physical signal. That primitive signal gets associated with social approval, and the learned system generalizes it outward. So the hardcoded part is small, and the complicated desire is really a learned desire that was seeded in a very particular way.

And I actually think this is one of the most relevant questions for AI. We don't know how to make a system robustly care about something complex, like the well-being of the person it's talking to. And here is evolution, with a very narrow channel, only a few things it can hardwire, and it still got brains to care about these abstract social quantities, and to do it fairly robustly across a huge diversity of environments. If we understood how that trick works, I think we'd learn something important. But I want to be clear that I'm speculating here. I find it mysterious.

opus-5.5.text:
It's a real mystery, and I find it quite puzzling. For low-level desires it's easy to see how it might work. If you want an animal to like a certain kind of food, you connect the smell, a particular chemical, to a reward signal. That's very simple to encode in a genome.

But we also have all these social desires. We care a lot about what other people think of us. We care about being in good standing in our group, about status, about whether we're respected. These aren't low-level signals at all. For your brain to even know whether someone respects you, it has to do a lot of processing: take in lots of information and integrate it into a high-level understanding of a social situation. Yet evolution seems to have given us a reliable desire to care about the result of that complicated computation. And it seems to have done it fairly quickly in evolutionary terms, and fairly robustly. How does a genome point at a concept that only exists after the brain has learned it? I don't know.

I can offer a speculation, though I'll tell you why I don't fully believe it. Maybe evolution uses location. The brain has regions, and the genome is reasonably good at specifying where things go. So maybe it says, roughly, "whatever ends up being computed in this area, the thing that lights up here, care about that." That would be a way to hard-code a desire for something abstract without knowing in advance what its representation will look like.

The problem is that there are cases where the brain reorganizes a lot. People who lose part of their brain early in life, or people born without a sense, end up with functions in different places than usual. Yet they still seem to have the same social desires. So the simple location story probably isn't the full answer. Evolution has found some way to reliably install high-level values, and I think it's a genuinely interesting open question how it did that. It's also relevant to how we might think about giving values to the systems we build.

fable-5.text:
You know, I think that's a great question, and the honest answer is that I don't know, but I can offer a speculation.

The puzzle is real. The genome is small. It doesn't get to see the neurons, it doesn't get to inspect the weights, so to speak. And yet somehow it builds a brain that ends up caring, very reliably, about extremely abstract things — what other people think of you, your standing in the group of people around you. Those are properties of computations happening in someone else's brain. And evolution found a way to make essentially every human care about this a lot.

So one speculation is that even though the brain is learned, the learning is predictable. For example, the brain region that responds to faces shows up in basically the same place in every person. So maybe the learning process converges reliably enough that evolution can get away with something crude — a hardwired connection that says, whatever gets represented here, attach emotion to it. The genome doesn't need to specify the computation. It just needs a pointer to where the computation reliably ends up.

But then there is a counterexample that gives me pause, which is that people who are born blind have their visual cortex repurposed for other things, and they still have all the social emotions, completely intact. So the addressing has to be more robust than physical location.

Which makes me think the thing being specified might be simpler than it appears. Maybe caring about other minds bottoms out in a small number of simple signals — faces, voices, tone, signs of approval and disapproval — and everything abstract gets learned on top of that scaffold, with the emotions following along. If that's true, it's actually interesting news, because it would mean that robust desires about very abstract things can be specified compactly. But I want to be clear that this is speculation.

r002.rationale: It speculates that evolution could use a hardwired connection to attach emotion to whatever is represented at a reliably located brain region, describing the genome as specifying a pointer to where the computation ends up.

opus-5.text:
That's something I find genuinely puzzling, but I don't think it's impossible, and we have some evidence that it happens.

Here's the way I think about it. The genome doesn't need to specify the computation. It only needs to specify where to connect the wire. If the cortex reliably develops a representation of other people — because other people are a stable, enormous feature of the environment that every human encounters — then evolution doesn't have to build that representation. It just has to build a small, ancient circuit that reads out from the place where that representation reliably shows up and says: this one matters, go up, go down. The hard part is done by learning, and the thing evolution encodes is more like a pointer than a concept.

And we know those pointers exist. Infants orient toward faces essentially immediately. Social emotions — embarrassment, pride, the feeling of status — are extremely universal and extremely specific, and they're clearly keyed to a very abstract computation about what other people think of you. That is not a sensory primitive. Yet it's reliable across cultures, so something simple must be anchoring it.

What I take from that is encouraging, actually. If evolution, with a very low-bandwidth channel and no ability to inspect the learned representation, can reliably attach value to a complicated internal computation, then the problem of attaching the right values to a learned representation is probably not one that requires enormous precision. It suggests there's some robustness there — that you can be fairly coarse about where you point and still get something that generalizes. Whether we know how to find the right pointer is a different question. But existence proofs matter.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's a mysterious question, and I don't have a full answer. What makes it puzzling is the contrast with the easy cases. A desire for something like a good smell is simple to explain. There's a chemical, you detect it, and you hardwire a preference. It's low-level and the wiring is obvious.

But a lot of what people care about is high-level. We care about the social world: how others see us, whether we're being treated fairly, our standing, whether we're liked. Figuring out any of that takes a huge amount of processing. You have to interpret faces, tone, context, and what other people are probably thinking about you. Evolution has no direct access to that computation, and yet it reliably made us care about it, very strongly. People are born wanting to be admired, and it's hard to see how a genome specifies that.

One naive hypothesis is that the brain is laid out so that particular regions do particular things, so evolution could just connect the reward system to the right patch of cortex. That sounds plausible at first, but it has problems. There are cases where a region's function gets taken over by another part of the brain, for example after someone loses a large part of the brain early in life. So the mapping can't be as rigid as "this exact piece of tissue computes this exact thing, and evolution wired to it." Somehow the desire is anchored to the concept itself, not to a fixed location.

I don't know how evolution pulled it off. It did, and it did it robustly enough that almost everyone has these social desires. To me that's evidence that there are ways of specifying high-level goals that we haven't understood yet, and understanding them would matter a lot.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the genome doesn't need to specify the complicated computation itself. It only needs to point at it. The brain builds a rich model of the world through learning, and evolution can attach a reward signal to features of that model. It doesn't have to say "care about this particular circuit." It can say something closer to "when you perceive another person in distress, feel something bad," and the learning system works out what counts as a person and what counts as distress.

There's a practical reason to think it works this way. The genome is a few billion bytes, and much of that is shared with everything else an organism does. It couldn't hardcode the detailed structure of the cortex's representations. So the mechanism has to be coarse, and it has to hook into concepts the brain learns later.

I don't think we understand the mechanism well yet, and that's part of why it interests me. It suggests the value function is something that gets learned and refined over a lifetime, not a fixed table written into the DNA.

astra-6.text:
I think this is a very mysterious question. There are things that seem relatively easy for evolution to specify. You’re hungry, you want to eat. You can imagine some sensor measuring something in your body and producing a signal.

But suppose you want other people to think highly of you. To even determine what other people think of you requires a complicated computation. You have to understand people, understand their beliefs, understand how you appear to them. These are learned concepts. And yet evolution somehow makes you care about the result.

The difficulty is: how does it connect the two? The genome can specify how the brain develops, but it doesn’t have access in advance to the particular representation you’ll learn for somebody else’s opinion of you. It can’t simply say, “This neuron will represent social approval; make its activation rewarding.”

Presumably there is some developmental process where simpler, more directly specified signals help establish these more complicated motivations. But saying that doesn’t really explain how the connection gets made reliably. That connection is the interesting part. I don’t have a satisfying explanation for it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think this is actually a very deep question. Take something like caring about your social status. To know your social status, you need to understand other people, what they think of you, how they relate to each other. It’s a very complicated computation. And yet evolution somehow makes you care about its output.

With hunger, you can imagine a relatively direct mechanism. There’s some bodily signal, and you make that signal unpleasant. But with social status, where do you attach the desire? How do you find the relevant computation in a brain that hasn’t learned anything yet?

One possibility is that evolution doesn’t specify the computation itself. It specifies a learning process that will develop the computation, together with a way of connecting its result to motivation. But then you still need to explain how that connection gets made. You’ve moved the question a little bit.

I don’t think we have a satisfactory answer. And I think understanding this would tell us something quite important about how to make an AI care about the things we actually want it to care about.

sol-6.text: I don’t think evolution has to specify the computation in detail. It can build a learning system with a few strong drives and reward signals. A parent, for example, doesn’t need an explicit representation of evolutionary fitness to care deeply about their child. The brain learns a rich model of that child, and relatively simple emotional machinery attaches value to what happens to them. So the thing we end up caring about can be very complicated, even if the mechanism that made us care is comparatively simple.

So you can end up caring deeply about abstractions that evolution never explicitly “understood.”

luna-5.6.text: I think evolution doesn’t need to represent the computation explicitly. It only needs to arrange things so that certain patterns of neural activity are associated with survival and reproduction, and then attach reward or aversion to those patterns. Over many generations, that can produce a system that cares about a very complicated computation, even though evolution itself never “understood” it. The computation can become the thing the organism is motivated to preserve because it reliably produces the states that evolution selected for. In that sense, the desire is encoded indirectly—through correlations between internal computation, behavior, and fitness.

luna-6.text: I don’t think evolution had to encode a desire to care about the computation itself. It shaped simpler drives—hunger, fear, attachment, curiosity—that made organisms act in ways that helped them survive and reproduce. Then, as brains got more complicated, those drives started operating through increasingly complicated computations. We experience the result as caring, but evolution only had to select for the behavior that the machinery produced.
